2. Brief facts of the case, giving rise to the present appeal, are as under:
2.1.
The alleged incident has taken place in the early morning of 14/04/1998.
As per the version of the complainant, on 13/04/1998, after coming of his from his service and taking meals, they had gone to sleep.
At about 4:00 a.m. his wife breaks his sleep and informed him that baby Fazila is not there.
They informed their relatives about the same.
One Yusuf Gulam Mohmad informed the complainant that at about 2:30 a.m. he had wake up to answer the nature's call and at that time ha hed seen one truck standing near his house on public road.
In the said truck he had Aiyub Manjra and Mahmad Hasan, present NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/118/2000 JUDGMENT DATED: 29/05/2025 undefined accused persons and one lady with her Burkha.
One person was also alleged to be standing on back side of the truck.

Subsequently when whereabouts of the preset accused was inquired by the complainant and his relatives, they were found not at their house and therefore the present complaint was lodged.
3. After registration of the FIR for the aforesaid offence against the accused, necessary investigation was carried out and statements of witnesses were recorded, panchnama was prepared as well as collected the medical evidences and FSL report.

During the course of investigation, as sufficient material was found against the accused, they was arrested and ultimately charge-sheet was filed against the respondent- accused before the concerned Magistrate Court.

However, as the case being exclusively sessions triable, the same was committed before the Sessions Court, Bharuch as per Section 209 of the Code of Criminal Procedure where the case was registered as Sessions Case No.160 of 1998.

4. On production of the respondent-accused and complying with the provisions of Section 207 of the Cr.P.C., charge was NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/118/2000 JUDGMENT DATED: 29/05/2025 undefined framed of the alleged offence against the respondent-accused but the accused has pleaded not guilty.

22. At the outset, it is required to be noted that the principles which would govern and regulate the hearing of appeal by this Court against an order of acquittal passed by the trial Court, have been very succinctly explained by the Apex Court in a catena of decisions.
In the case of M.S. Narayana Menon @ Mani Vs. State of Kerala & Anr., (2006) 6 S.C.C. 39, the Apex Court has narrated the powers of High Court in appeal against the order of acquittal.

In Paragraph-54 of the said decision, the Apex Court has observed as under:
NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/118/2000 JUDGMENT DATED: 29/05/2025 undefined "54.
In any event the High Court entertained an appeal treating to be an appeal against acquittal, it was in fact exercising the revisional jurisdiction.

Even while exercising an appellate power against a judgment of acquittal, the High Court should have borne in mind the well-settled principles of law that where two view are possible, the appellate Court should not interfere with the finding of acquittal recorded by the Court below."

entities.text: Chandrappa Vs. State of Karnataka, (2007) 4 S.C.C. 415
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
From the above decisions, in our considered view, the following general principles regarding powers of the appellate Court while dealing with an appeal State Of Gujarat vs Mohmed Hasan Kaiyat on 29 May, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/91142283/
6 against an order of acquittal emerge:
[1] An appellate Court has full power to review, re- appreciate and reconsider the evidence upon which the order of acquittal is founded.
[2] The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 puts no limitation, restriction or condition on exercise of such power and an appellate Court on the evidence before it may reach its own conclusion, both on questions of fact and of law.

sentences.text: [ 3 ] Various expressions, such as, "substantial and compelling reasons", "good and sufficient grounds", "very strong circumstances", "distorted conclusions", "glaring mistakes", etc. are not intended to curtain extensive powers of an appellate Court in an appeal against acquittal.

Such phraseologies are more in the nature of "flourishes of language" to emphasis the reluctance of an appellate Court to interfere with NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/118/2000 JUDGMENT DATED: 29/05/2025 undefined acquittal than to curtail the power of the Court to review the evidence and to come to its own conclusion.
[4] An appellate Court, however, must bear in mind that in case of acquittal there is double presumption in favour of the accused.

Firstly, the presumption of innocence is available to him under the fundamental principle of criminal jurisprudence that every person shall be presumed to be innocent unless he is proved guilty by a competent Court of law.
Secondly, the accused having secured his acquittal, the presumption of his innocence is further reinforced, reaffirmed and strengthened by the trial Court.

[5] If two reasonable conclusions are possible on the basis of the evidence on record,
the appellate Court should not disturb the finding of acquittal recorded by the trial Court."
22.2.

Thus, it is a settled principle that while exercising appellate power, even if two reasonable conclusions are possible on the basis of the evidence on record, the appellate Court should not disturb the finding of acquittal recorded by the trial Court.
22.3. In the case of State of Goa V. Sanjay Thakran & Anr., (2007) 3 S.C.C. 75, the Apex Court reiterated the powers of the High Court in such cases.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In Paragraph-16 of the said decision, the Court observed as under;
"16.

From the aforesaid decisions, it is apparent that NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/118/2000 JUDGMENT DATED: 29/05/2025 undefined while exercising the powers in appeal against the order of acquittal the Court of appeal would not ordinarily interfere with the order of acquittal unless the approach of the lower Court is vitiated by some manifest illegality and the conclusion arrived at would not be arrived at by any reasonable person and, therefore, the decision is to be characterized as perverse.

Merely because two views are possible, the Court of appeal would not State Of Gujarat vs Mohmed Hasan Kaiyat on 29 May, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/91142283/
7 take the view which would upset the judgment delivered by the Court below.

sentences.text: However, the appellate Court has a power to review the evidence if it is of the view that the conclusion arrived at by the Court below is perverse and the Court has committed a manifest error of law and ignored the material evidence on record.

A duty is cast upon the appellate Court, in such circumstances, to re- appreciate the evidence to arrive to a just decision on the basis of material placed on record to find out whether any of the accused is connected with the commission of the crime he is charged with."
22.4.

Similar principle has been laid down by the Apex Court in the cases of State of Uttar Pradesh Vs. Ram Veer Singh & Ors, 2007 A.I.R. S.C.W. 5553 and in Girja Prasad (Dead) by LRs Vs. State of MP reported in 2007 A.I.R. S.C.W. 5589.

22.5. It is also a settled legal position that in acquittal appeal, the appellate Court is not required to re-write the judgment or to give fresh reasonings, when the reasons assigned by the Court below are found to be just and proper.

Such principle is NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/118/2000 JUDGMENT DATED: 29/05/2025 undefined laid down by the Apex Court in the case of State of Karnataka Vs. Hemareddy reported in AIR 1981 S.C. 1417, wherein, it is held as under:
"... This Court has observed in Girija Nandini Devi V. Bigendra Nandini Chaudhary (1967)1 SCR 93: (AIR 1967 SC 1124) that it is not the duty of the appellate Court when it agrees with the view of the trial Court on the evidence to repeat the narration of the evidence or to reiterate the reasons given by the trial Court expression of general agreement with the reasons given by the Court the decision of which is under appeal,
will ordinarily suffice."

sentences.text: 22.6. Thus, in case the appellate Court agrees with the reasons and the opinion given by the lower Court, then the discussion of evidence is not necessary.

23. Considering the impugned judgment and order of the learned trial Court and the aforesaid reasoning and bearing in mind the statutory provisions, as well as the judgments of the Hon'ble Apex Court, this Court is of the considered opinion that the present appeal does not warrant any interference in the impugned judgment and order passed by the learned trial Court.

We find that the findings recorded by the learned trial Court are absolutely just and proper and in recording the said NEUTRAL CITATION R/CR.A/118/2000 JUDGMENT DATED: 29/05/2025 undefined findings, no illegality and infirmity has been committed by it.
We are therefore, in complete agreement with the findings and ultimate conclusion recorded by the learned trial Court and there is no reasons to interfere with the same.
24. The present appeal of the State is accordingly dismissed.
Bail bond, if any, shall stand cancelled.
25. Record and proceedings be sent back forthwith to the concerned court.
